overview: Akawaio, also spelled Akawayo, identifies Indigenous Cariban-speaking communities of the Guiana Highlands. Their histories overlap with neighboring peoples without making those peoples interchangeable. Historical collectors used names inconsistently, so objects labeled Akawaio, Patamona or Kapon require attention to their particular collection records.

periods.title: Communities map their territory
periods.summary: Akawaio and Arekuna communities began a participatory mapping project in 1995 and published their map in 1998. They combined local place names and land-use knowledge with geographic positioning. The project documented their claims; its boundaries have not been substituted for this atlas’s imported polygon.

periods.title: Continuing council and community work
periods.summary: The Upper Mazaruni District Council brought village leaders together at Waramadong in October 2025 to discuss services, environmental problems and collective representation. This continuing institution is documented long after the map’s brief historical interval.

items.text: A basket sieve called tonga, NMAI_61541, combines twill-plaited plant fibers with wood and cordage. The museum records it from the Lower Essequibo and says Verrill collected it in 1916. Its classification connects basketry to food preparation. That collection date does not establish when the object was made or when the technique began.

A food grater from the Upper Cuyuni, NMAI_214381, brings together carved wood, stone and tree pitch or gum. The record tentatively associates its collection with a 1937 or 1938 expedition and records its donation in 1939. These materials document a composite household tool; the uncertain collecting history should not become a precise manufacture date.

Bulkan’s 2019 comparison emphasizes women’s knowledge and work in transforming bitter cassava into food and drink. The study distinguishes the Makushi and Akawaio cases. Its detailed discussion of Makushi plant varieties cannot simply be transferred to all Akawaio gardens, but the comparison shows why food history includes skills and social responsibilities.

The same study describes eki siku, an Akawaio young-cassava festival within the areruya religious tradition. Cassava and women’s roles are affirmed through sacred texts and prophetic visions. The account treats cultivation, belief and social relationships together, rather than reducing a staple crop to its nutritional value.

The 2014 dictionary was developed with Akawaio speakers from the Upper Mazaruni and linguists Ray and Dee Stegeman. Its introduction describes work on an alphabet, reading books and a lexical database. Recording pronunciations, meanings and alternative forms makes a practical resource for speakers and learners while preserving variation within the language.

The dictionary records simari, with the variant sumari, for a cassava grater. Its si’na’ entry describes both a tree whose inner bark supplies carrying straps and the straps themselves. These entries connect vocabulary with material knowledge and transport. They do not identify a botanical species or date the origin of either tool.

Clarke’s botanical expedition report credits Akawaio Isaac Jerry and Adrian Thompson with establishing a western route up Mount Ayanganna from Chinowieng. Earlier scientific parties used that route. Naming the guide makes visible the local geographic expertise on which collecting expeditions depended, rather than treating a scientific visit as the first human knowledge of a landscape.

For the mapping project begun in 1995, Indigenous team members learned surveying and GPS methods. Communities supplied names and categories for settlements, resource areas, burial grounds and other significant places. Griffiths’s account explains how younger people worked with Elders, turning knowledge normally transmitted locally into a map that outsiders could examine.

The published map made land uses visible that official maps could overlook, including hunting and fishing reserves. Griffiths reported that the government had not accepted it as a legitimate ownership claim when he wrote in 2002. Producing evidence and winning legal recognition were different steps; the map alone did not settle the dispute.

At the 2025 Waramadong meeting, village representatives discussed social, environmental and economic concerns with public agencies. Leaders also renewed a request for formal recognition of their District Council. This is evidence of active collective decision-making, not a claim that official recognition had already been granted.

In 2026, the Upper Mazaruni council joined other Indigenous councils in training on digital mapping and data management. Participants practiced collecting, organizing and interpreting information and preparing reports. These methods support community monitoring and advocacy, showing the continued adoption of new tools alongside local knowledge.

ending.text: Akawaio communities continue to organize, maintain knowledge and pursue recognition of their institutions and land rights. The 2025 council meeting documents ongoing work, not a completed settlement of every claim. The map’s 1500 endpoint is a coverage limit and does not mark a conquest or the disappearance of the people.
